name: Character Voice and Dialogue
title: Character Voice and Dialogue
answer: Character voice and dialogue covers the craft of making a fictional person sound like themselves on the page, in a script, or in a game, and it now includes the use of language models to draft, extend, or test that speech. The work sits at the meeting point of literary arts and narrative design, where a novelist, screenwriter, or game writer decides not only what a character says but how they say it, what they avoid, and how their speech shifts under pressure. In interactive work the same material becomes a system, since a character may need to speak across thousands of possible player states rather than along one fixed path.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Most practitioners work in ordinary writing tools, from word processors and screenwriting software to game dialogue editors and branching narrative engines, with a language model used alongside as a drafting or variation partner. Audio enters the picture when a voice performance or a synthetic voice is layered onto the written line, and the site currently tracks 2000 audio models, a reminder of how much of this craft now ends in sound rather than text alone. A writer may keep a character bible, a sample of past lines, and a set of constraints that are pasted into a model to keep a voice consistent across sessions.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The usual method starts with a voice sheet: vocabulary, rhythm, sentence length, verbal tics, topics the character dodges, and how they speak to people of different status. A model is then asked for alternatives, continuations, or reactions to a specific scene, and the writer selects, edits, and rewrites rather than accepting output whole. Testing matters as much as drafting, so lines are read aloud, run past other writers, or played through a scene to check that the voice holds when the character is angry, lying, or tired. In games, the same lines are checked against branching paths so that a voice does not collapse when the player chooses an unexpected route.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights questions cluster around two things: the source material a model was trained on and the ownership of what it produces. A writer who feeds a living author's novels into a model to imitate a style is in different territory from one who prompts for a generic tone, and the site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, which shows how unsettled these lines still are. Provenance practices are emerging in response, including keeping records of prompts, drafts, and edits, disclosing model use where a publisher or studio requires it, and treating a synthetic voice clone as a separate consent issue from the text itself. Voice actors and writers have raised concerns about replacement, and contracts increasingly address whether generated dialogue or cloned performance can be used.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The likely direction is toward tools that hold a character voice across long projects, remember prior lines, and flag when a new line drifts from the established register. That pushes the writer's job further toward judgment, curation, and the design of constraints rather than the production of every first draft. Interactive and audio work will probably absorb the change fastest, given how much dialogue those forms require and how directly synthetic speech can be inserted. The open questions are less technical than social: who is credited, who is paid, and how a distinctive human voice is protected when it can be approximated from a modest sample.
